paras: The killing of Joe Ross was the fatal shooting of Joe Ross, a Black man also known as Joe Wilson, by ferryman Alonzo Huntley at Ivy's Mill on the Catawba River in Lancaster County, South Carolina, on the night of December 6, 1882. Ross was being hunted by a party of Camden citizens as the accused killer of F. N. McDowell, and they had posted the ferryman at the crossing. Wire services carried the news across the country, and North Carolina papers hailed it as revenge for two killings Ross was said to have confessed.

On Thanksgiving morning, November 30, McDowell was killed with an axe about thirteen miles above Camden, and his body was found in a ditch covered with brush. Papers named the accused as Joe Wilson, a Black man who had worked for McDowell, and the Alexandria Gazette predicted that if he was caught 'it is not improbable that he will be lynched.' According to the Charlotte Observer, McDowell had twice had him jailed over mortgaged property and twice taken him out on a promise to work.

When the pursuers visited his brother, Tom Wilson, he told them that Joe Wilson was Joe Ross, wanted for the killing of Bob Hennegan in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, two years earlier, with a $200 reward offered by the Governor. The Observer wrote that 300 citizens set out 'with the determination not to return home without his body, dead or alive.'

After a fruitless search around Charlotte, a party of twenty-five turned back into Lancaster County, where Black cotton pickers near Six Mile church and children at a nearby cabin told them that a man of Ross's description had gone toward Ivy's Mill. Hemmed in by Sugar Creek and the Catawba, Ross went to the ferryman's house and asked to be taken across.

In the Observer's account, Huntley recognized him, invited him to warm himself at the fire, then picked up a musket and told him he was under arrest. Ross sprang at the gun and pulled out its ramrod, and Huntley shot him in the back just above the thigh. Huntley tied him and called in the searchers, among them Ross's brother, who was quoted as saying, 'They've got you at last.'

The party carried Ross by wagon to the old Hagan house, an unoccupied building, and laid him on straw, where one of them wrote down what the papers called his confession to both killings. He died early the next morning, at 3 o'clock by two accounts and 5 o'clock by the Observer's.

The body was taken by wagon to Lancaster and then to Camden to be delivered to McDowell's brother. The Observer expected Huntley to collect the Governor's reward, and no report of an inquest or of any legal action over the shooting appears in the coverage.

A Charlotte dispatch of December 7, also sent under a Camden dateline, ran in papers from New York to Sacramento and Albuquerque under headlines such as 'A Negro Murderer Killed,' stating only that 'Ross resisted, and the ferryman shot him.'

In South Carolina, a Charleston News and Courier dispatch from Rock Hill, headed 'The Murder of a Murderer' in the Anderson Intelligencer, placed the killing near Fort Mill and said that the Camden 'gentlemen' had posted the ferryman. The Charlotte Messenger gave the news in one line, calling Ross 'the outlaw.'

The fullest accounts came from Charlotte: the Observer story, reprinted in Raleigh as 'The Slayer Slain!' beside a brief headed 'REVENGED AT LAST!', described an 'avenging band' running its 'game' to bay and printed the dying man's confession at length. The Charlotte Home and Democrat closed its account, 'Thus ends the career of a desperate murderer.' Every account treated the accusations as fact, and all of them came from the pursuers' side.

The Rock Hill dispatch said the encounter began because the ferryman refused to put Ross across, while the Charlotte accounts described a planned arrest at the fireside. The Yorkville Enquirer dated the capture to 'last Thursday' rather than Wednesday night, and the Observer gave the size of the tracking party as twenty-five against the three hundred who first set out.

reader.title: Killing of Joe Ross
bases: A party of private citizens hunting Ross as an accused murderer had posted the ferryman who shot him while trying to arrest him; Ross died of the wound in the party's hands (A10, A11, A14, A17).

Ross was killed by one man, ferryman Alonzo Huntley, who shot him when Ross grabbed at his musket during an attempted arrest of a fugitive with a reward on him; the pursuing party of 25 or more arrived only after the shooting and no paper reports further violence by them (A11, A14, A17). The party had set out to bring him back 'dead or alive' and had posted the ferryman (A10, A12), but the papers tell only the captors' side of the shooting.

A Charlotte wire, a Charleston News and Courier dispatch from Rock Hill, the Charlotte Observer account and South Carolina and Charlotte local papers independently agree that a ferryman shot Ross at the Catawba crossing as his pursuers closed in (A5, A11, A14, A15, A17).

Distant papers ran the Charlotte or Camden wire under 'A Negro Murderer Killed' or 'Shot', treating the accusation as fact.
The Charlotte Messenger gave a single line calling Ross 'the outlaw'.
